result.markdown: --- title: "Session 3 — Overdispersion" subtitle: "Dispersion statistic · quasi-Poisson · negative binomial · robust standard errors · Lab 3" author: "Community Medicine Workshop" format: revealjs: theme: serif css: [../assets/slide_deck.css, assets/workshop.css, assets/quiz.css] include-after-body: assets/quiz-include.html embed-resources: true slide-number: true navigation-mode: linear code-copy: true center: false transition: fade width: 1280 height: 720 fig-align: center html-math-method: plain execute: echo: true warning: false message: false fig-width: 9 fig-height: 4.6 fig-dpi: 100 --- ## Where we are ::: {.incremental} - Session 2: Poisson regression and rate ratios - Today: when the data are **more variable than a Poisson allows**, which is **usual** - By the end you can: - **measure** overdispersion - choose between **quasi-Poisson**, **negative binomial** and **robust SEs** - see why **standard errors**, not estimates, are the problem ::: # Topic 1 — Detecting it {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## The dispersion statistic ::: {.eq} dispersion = sum of squared Pearson residuals / residual df (about **1** if Poisson fits) ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m2 <- glm(cases ~ fogging + slum + rain_lag1 + month_index + sin(2 * pi * month / 12) + cos(2 * pi * month / 12) + offset(log(population)), family = poisson, data = dg) sum(residuals(m2, type = "pearson")^2) / df.residual(m2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 7.938899 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} check_overdispersion(m2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # Overdispersion test dispersion ratio = 7.939 Pearson's Chi-Squared = 8518.439 p-value = < 0.001 ``` ::: ::: ## What dispersion means ::: {.warn} A dispersion of **7.9** means the Poisson **standard errors are too small by about its square root (2.8 times)**. The coefficients are still reasonable; the **p-values and CIs are not**. ::: ## Why is count data overdispersed? ::: {.incremental} - **Unmeasured heterogeneity:** wards differ in ways we did not record - **Clustering:** events cluster in space and time (outbreaks) - **Contagion:** one case causes others (not independent) - **Zero inflation** (Session 4) ::: # Topic 2 — Three remedies {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Quasi-Poisson ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m_q <- glm(formula(m2), family = quasipoisson, data = dg) round(cbind(Poisson_SE = summary(m2)$coefficients[, 2], Quasi_SE = summary(m_q)$coefficients[, 2])[2:3, ], 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Poisson_SE Quasi_SE foggingYes 0.032 0.090 slumSlum 0.020 0.056 ``` ::: ::: Same **coefficients**, standard errors **multiplied by sqrt(dispersion)**. Simple; no AIC (not a full likelihood). ## Negative binomial ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m_nb <- MASS::glm.nb(formula(m2), data = dg) c(theta = round(m_nb$theta, 2)); AIC(m2, m_nb) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` theta 1.4 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` df AIC m2 7 10744.836 m_nb 8 5898.446 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.eq} Var(Y) = mu + mu^2^ / theta ::: ::: {.incremental} - An extra parameter **theta** lets the variance grow **faster than the mean**; **smaller theta = more overdispersion** - A real likelihood: compare models by **AIC** - The usual first choice for overdispersed counts ::: ## Rate ratios compared ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bind_rows(Poisson = tidy(m2, conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE), NB = tidy(m_nb, conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE), .id = "model") |> filter(term == "foggingYes") |> select(model, RR = estimate, low = conf.low, high = conf.high) |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 4 model RR low high 1 Poisson 0.64 0.6 0.68 2 NB 0.66 0.54 0.8 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.key} The **point estimate** barely moves; the **CI is about three times wider** with the negative binomial. Do not report the Poisson CI when the data are overdispersed. ::: ## Robust (clustered) standard errors ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} coeftest(m2, vcov = vcovCL(m2, cluster = dg$ward))[2:3, ] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|) foggingYes -0.4533550 0.1199850 -3.778432 0.0001578192 slumSlum 0.5362063 0.1688614 3.175423 0.0014961816 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.incremental} - The same ward appears **36 times**: observations are **correlated** - `vcovCL(model, cluster = ward)` gives **cluster-robust** standard errors, valid for **correlated** data - Use with Poisson (rates stay the same, SEs honest) or with NB ::: # Topic 3 — Choosing {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Which one? | Option | Use when | Gives | |---|---|---| | **Poisson** | dispersion near 1 | rate ratios, AIC | | **Quasi-Poisson** | overdispersed, only SEs matter | rate ratios, corrected SE, no AIC | | **Negative binomial** | overdispersed (usual) | rate ratios, AIC, theta | | **Robust SE** | clustering (repeated wards) | honest SE for any of these | | Mixed model (random ward effect) | clustering and ward-level heterogeneity | beyond this workshop | ## 🔧 Switch to R — Lab 3 {.lab-slide background-color="#1565c0"} ::: {.lab-box} **File:** `counts-workshop/labs/lab3_overdisp.R` - dispersion by hand and with `check_overdispersion()` - `quasipoisson` and `MASS::glm.nb()` - `vcovCL()` clustered by ward ::: **Time:** 40 minutes · answer the Q questions in the comments ## Self-check quiz (1/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="s3q1" data-type="mcq" data-hash="jtwbia.so757r" data-show="VGhlIG1vZGVsIGhhcyB0b28gZmV3IHByZWRpY3RvcnMgdG8gZGVzY3JpYmUgdGhlIGNvdW50 cw==" data-explain="T3ZlcmRpc3BlcnNpb24gbGVhdmVzIHRoZSBjb2VmZmljaWVudCBlc3RpbWF0ZXMgcm91Z2hs eSBzZW5zaWJsZSBidXQgdW5kZXJzdGF0ZXMgdGhlaXIgdW5jZXJ0YWludHk6IHRoZSBTRXMg c2hvdWxkIGJlIGluZmxhdGVkIGJ5IGFib3V0IHRoZSBzcXVhcmUgcm9vdCBvZiB0aGUgZGlz cGVyc2lvbi4="} A Poisson model has a dispersion statistic of 8. What is the main consequence? - Standard errors are too small, so p-values are over-optimistic - The coefficients are wrong by a factor of 8 in every model - The model has too few predictors to describe the counts - The offset has been specified incorrectly in the model formula ::: ## Self-check quiz (2/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="s3q2" data-type="mcq" data-hash="jtwoqy.so7jp3" data-show="VGhlIGludGVyY2VwdCBvZiB0aGUgbW9kZWwsIHdoaWNoIHNldHMgdGhlIGJhc2VsaW5lIHJh dGU=" data-explain="VmFyaWFuY2UgPSBtdSArIG11XjIvdGhldGEsIHNvIGEgc21hbGwgdGhldGEgbWVhbnMgdmFy aWFuY2UgZmFyIGFib3ZlIHRoZSBtZWFuIGFuZCBhIGxhcmdlIHRoZXRhIGFwcHJvYWNoZXMg YSBQb2lzc29uLg=="} Which parameter of the negative binomial measures overdispersion? - theta: the smaller it is, the more overdispersion there is - The intercept of the model, which sets the baseline rate - The offset, because it holds the variance of the counts - The p-value of the dispersion test, which grows with variance ::: ## Self-check quiz (3/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="s3q3" data-type="mcq" data-hash="jtx1zo.so7y6h" data-show="VGhlIHN0YW5kYXJkIGVycm9ycywgd2l0aCB0aGUgc2FtZSBjb2VmZmljaWVudHM=" data-explain="UXVhc2ktUG9pc3NvbiBlc3RpbWF0ZXMgdGhlIGRpc3BlcnNpb24gYW5kIG11bHRpcGxpZXMg dGhlIHZhcmlhbmNlcyBieSBpdDogY29lZmZpY2llbnRzIGFyZSBpZGVudGljYWwsIHN0YW5k YXJkIGVycm9ycyBhcmUgaW5mbGF0ZWQu"} Compared with the Poisson model, what does quasi-Poisson change? - The coefficients, with the same standard errors - The link function from log to identity - The standard errors, with the same coefficients - The number of observations used ::: ## Self-check quiz (4/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="s3q4" data-type="mcq" data-hash="jtxf8e.so8cnv" data-show="UG9pc3NvbiBtb2RlbHMgbmVlZCBvbmUgc2luZ2xlIHJvdyBmb3IgZWFjaCB3YXJkIGluIHRo ZSBmaWxl" data-explain="UmVwZWF0ZWQgbW9udGhzIHdpdGhpbiBhIHdhcmQgYXJlIG5vdCBpbmRlcGVuZGVudCwgc28g dGhlcmUgaXMgbGVzcyBpbmZvcm1hdGlvbiB0aGFuIDEsMDgwIGluZGVwZW5kZW50IG9ic2Vy dmF0aW9ucy4gQ2x1c3RlcmVkIFNFcyBhY2NvdW50IGZvciB0aGlzLg=="} Why use cluster-robust standard errors by ward here? - The same ward is measured 36 times, so observations are correlated - Wards are too small to be analysed with any count model - Robust standard errors remove overdispersion from the estimates - Poisson models need one single row for each ward in the file ::: ## Self-check quiz (5/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="s3q5" data-type="mcq" data-hash="jtxsh0.so8r55" data-show="VGhlIG5lZ2F0aXZlIGJpbm9taWFsIGZpdHMgZmFyIGJldHRlcg==" data-explain="TG93ZXIgQUlDIG1lYW5zIGEgYmV0dGVyIHRyYWRlLW9mZiBvZiBmaXQgYW5kIGNvbXBsZXhp dHkuIEEgZGlmZmVyZW5jZSBvZiB0aG91c2FuZHMgaXMgb3ZlcndoZWxtaW5nIGV2aWRlbmNl IGZvciB0aGUgbmVnYXRpdmUgYmlub21pYWwu"} AIC is 10,745 for the Poisson model and 5,898 for the negative binomial on the same data. What do you conclude? - The negative binomial fits far better - The two models fit equally well - The Poisson model is better because it has fewer parameters - AIC cannot be compared between these models ::: ## Score and take-home **Your score: ** ::: {.incremental} - Check **dispersion** (about 1 if Poisson); overdispersion is **usual** - **Negative binomial** (or quasi-Poisson) fixes the SEs; the estimates barely move - **Clustered robust SEs** for repeated units - Do not report **Poisson CIs** for overdispersed counts ::: **Next:** Session 4: zeros and model checking

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
